lessons.title: What a business is and how it is organised
lessons.html:
The purpose of a business

A business provides goods or services to customers in order to make a profit. A macadamia farm sells nut-in-shell to a cracking factory; a fruit packhouse grades and packs citrus for export; an abattoir slaughters livestock and sells meat. Each must earn more money than it spends to survive, pay workers and grow.

Forms of business ownership in South Africa

FormFeatures
Sole proprietorOne owner, simple to start, owner personally liable for debts
PartnershipTwo or more owners share profits and liability
Private company (Pty) LtdSeparate legal entity registered with CIPC, owners (shareholders) have limited liability
Co-operativeOwned and controlled by members, common among farmers for buying inputs and marketing produce

Business functions

  • Production: growing, harvesting, processing and packing.
  • Purchasing: buying inputs such as fertiliser, cartons and chemicals at the right price and quality.
  • Marketing and sales: finding customers, setting prices, meeting market standards.
  • Human resources: recruiting, training, paying and caring for staff.
  • Finance: managing money, budgets, records and payments.
  • Administration: records, communication and compliance.

All functions depend on each other. If purchasing orders the wrong cartons, the packhouse cannot pack, sales cannot deliver and finance does not get paid.

Vision, mission and goals

A vision says what the business wants to become, such as 'to be the most trusted macadamia supplier in Mpumalanga'. The mission says how. Goals are specific targets, like reducing reject nuts by 10% this season. Every worker contributes to these goals.

lessons.title: Money in a business: income, costs and profit
lessons.html:
Understanding the numbers

Income and costs

  • Income (revenue): money from sales, such as the price per kilogram of nuts or per carton of fruit.
  • Fixed costs: stay the same regardless of output, such as permanent salaries, insurance, loan repayments and rent.
  • Variable costs: change with output, such as packaging, seasonal labour, fuel and electricity used by processing lines.

Profit

Profit = income − total costs.

Example: a packhouse packs 20 000 cartons in a month and earns R95 per carton packed. Income = R1 900 000. Fixed costs are R600 000 and variable costs are R55 per carton (R1 100 000). Total costs = R1 700 000. Profit = R200 000.

Cost per unit

Dividing total cost by units produced shows efficiency. Here: R1 700 000 ÷ 20 000 = R85 per carton. If volume dropped to 15 000 cartons, fixed costs would be spread over fewer cartons and the cost per carton would rise. That is why throughput and avoiding downtime matter.

Records

Businesses keep records of sales, purchases, wages, stock and assets. Accurate records allow the owner to prepare financial statements, pay the correct tax to SARS, and make decisions. Supervisors contribute by keeping accurate timesheets, production figures and stock counts.

Budgets

A budget is a financial plan for a period. Managers compare actual figures with the budget each month. If packaging costs are higher than budgeted, they investigate: did prices rise, or was there more waste?

How workers affect profit

  • Reducing waste and rework
  • Caring for equipment to avoid breakdowns
  • Working safely to avoid injuries and lost time
  • Meeting quality standards so product is not rejected by customers

lessons.title: Customers, markets and responsible business
lessons.html:
Selling to the market

The marketing mix

Marketing is about meeting customer needs profitably. The four Ps:

  • Product: what is sold, its quality, grade, size and packaging.
  • Price: must cover costs, be competitive and reflect quality.
  • Place: how product reaches customers, such as fresh produce markets, export agents, retailers or direct sales.
  • Promotion: how customers learn about the product, such as trade shows, brand labels and relationships with buyers.

Supply and demand

Prices in agriculture often depend on supply and demand. When many farmers harvest at the same time, supply is high and prices tend to fall. When supply is short, for example after hail damage in a region, prices tend to rise. Exchange rates also affect export earnings.

Quality and standards

Export and retail customers set strict standards for size, colour, defects, residues and packaging. Certification schemes and audits check food safety and ethical practice. Product that does not meet the standard is rejected or sold at a lower price, which directly reduces income.

Responsible business

A sustainable business looks after more than profit:

  • People: fair wages, safe working conditions under the OHS Act 85 of 1993, training and respect.
  • Environment: protecting soil and water, using chemicals responsibly, managing waste.
  • Community: local employment and supporting local suppliers.
  • Compliance: following labour, tax, food safety and environmental law.

Entrepreneurship

Many successful agricultural businesses started small: a few hives, a vegetable tunnel or a small nursery. Basic business principles, such as knowing your costs, finding a reliable market and keeping records, apply to every size of business.

Key points

  • A business provides goods or services to make a profit.
  • Business functions such as production, purchasing, marketing, HR and finance depend on each other.
  • Profit = income − total costs; cost per unit shows efficiency.
  • The marketing mix is product, price, place and promotion.
  • Every worker affects profit through quality, waste, safety and care of equipment.
